catalog_quote: Buru genitive enclitics are non-syllabic –C. Kayeli genitive enclitics are more historically conservative, being syllabic –CV. The Kayeli enclitics are extrametrical, not affecting penultimate stress on the root. ... Buru uses a non-syllabic applicative –k suffix. Kayeli, on the other hand, uses a disyllabic stress bearing auxiliary heer that can also indicate a causative, and thus also affect the interpetation of the preverbal core argument.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the lexical root; the syllabic (CV) genitive enclitics that follow the root are extrametrical, i.e. they are ignored for stress assignment and do not shift the stress rightward (contrast Buru, where the enclitics are non-syllabic). A disyllabic auxiliary heer bears its own stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; enclitics are explicitly extrametrical
new_statements.domain_note: Stated in passing in a comparative Buru/Kayeli/Hukumina grammar section, not in a phonology chapter; domain is the phonological word (root + enclitics). Data are first-hand: Grimes elicited from the last four Kayeli speakers (Kayeli dialect, villages Kayeli/Masarete) in 1983 and 1989, holding a 700-item Kayeli list and a 205-item Leliali list.
new_statements.identity_note: Kayeli proper, kaye1241/kzl, the Kayeli dialect of the Kayeli language (villages Kayeli and Masarete, Namlea Bay, NE Buru). Grimes 1991/2000 treat Leliali (last speaker died March 1989) and Lumaete as dialects of Kayeli and, on indirect evidence only, Moksela (moks1249) too; Grimes's 700-item list and the 1995 paper's data come from the last four speakers of the Kayeli dialect, so the stress remark describes Kayeli proper. Holle list 55c and Wallace's list no. 21 are respectively Lisela-Buru (lise1239) and genuine Kayeli per Grimes.

sources.citation: Collins, James T. 1983. The historical relationships of the languages of Central Maluku, Indonesia. Pacific Linguistics D-47. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: No Kayeli stress location. pp.13-15 summarise Stresemann 1927: for 'Sub-Buru' 'the vowel preceding the stressed syllable is usually lost', and Kayeli is 'a sort of transitional language' showing 'unstressed vowel deletion characteristic of Buru' plus Sub-Ambon features; p.~82 'obligatory penultimate stress rule' concerns Hoamoal/Asilulu (Ambon-Seram), not Kayeli; p.~64 'Kayeli-Alfuren' stress-conditioned *a split is Stresemann's Buru-dialect data.

sources.citation: Grimes, Charles E. 2000. Defining speech communities on Buru Island: a look at both linguistic and non-linguistic factors. In C. E. Grimes (ed.), Spices from the east: papers in languages of eastern Indonesia, 73-103. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics 503.
sources.note: Nothing on Kayeli stress. Sec. 7.4.4 (pp.99-102) is a sociolinguistic/dialect orientation (Kayeli, Leliali, Lumaete dialects; Moksela possibly), identifies Holle list 55a and Wallace's 'Cajeli' as Kayeli, and mentions the author's 700-item Kayeli word list and 205-item Leliali list. Sound correspondences for Kayeli vs Buru only (PAn *R > Kayeli /l/, *p > /h/).

sources.note: Sec. 4.3.1 'Kayeli (Cajeli, Gaeli)' pp.31-33 is a sociolinguistic orientation (three dialects, speaker numbers, Holle/Wallace list identification); no Kayeli stress statement. Ch.5 'Stress' (5.2) describes Buru only (penultimate, enclitics do not shift stress); p.28 says Hukumina stress patterns differ strikingly from Buru and Kayeli.
